texts.preamble: M/S Jubilant Foodworks Ltd vs Sh. Bal Mukund on 13 March, 2023 In The Court Of Mr. Dharmesh Sharma Principal District & Sessions Judge / Food Safety Appellate Tribunal; New Delhi District Patiala House Courts : New Delhi Fsat No. 22/2018 Cnr No. Dlnd01137422018 1. M/s Jubilant Foodworks Ltd. Through A/R Mr. Rohit Singh B214, PhaseII District Gautam Budh Nagar Noida201305. 2. Sh. Akash Tyagi S/o Sh. Manoj Tyagi R/o 453/8, Durgapuri Extension Shahdara, Delhi110094. .....Appe Versus Sh. Bal Mukund, Food Safety Officer, 8th Floor, Mayur Bhawan New Delhi110001. ...... Respond
texts.facts: Briefly stated, it is the case of the appellants that M/s. Jubilant Food Works Ltd. is a company incorporated under the provisions of Companies Act, 1956 having its corporate office at B214, PhaseII, District Guatum Budh Nagar, Noida201305 and the appellant No.2 Sh. Akash Tyagi was working as Manager at its Restaurant viz., Domino's Pizza India Restaurant situated as N7, Connaught Place, New Delhi. It is stated that on 07.05.2014 at around 03:00 p.m. Mr. Bal Mukund, Food Safety Officer (FSO) accompanied with other staff of the department came at the aforesaid Domino's Pizza Outlet and directly approached the Kitchen area (situated separately from the Restaurant area) where food preparation processes were being carried out; and that the FSO started checking the Kitchen area and went to the shelf where raw Pizza bases were kept prepared by the cook and various ingredients in raw form were kept in the shelf and the FSO took one open container of 'Corn Meal' (which incidentally acknowledges as "Corn Flour" vide Form VA prepared by FSO) kept from the shelf kept for preparing the Pizza Base and took a sample of 'Corn Meal'. It is the case of the appellants that 'Corn Meal' is used as dusting agent while preparing the pizza base from the dough so that the dough should not stick with the shelf and the only purpose of the 'Corn Meal' is to act as facilitator against the sticky tendency of the dough and 'Corn Meal' is not mixed in any other product or preparation. It is stated that 'Corn Meal' placed in the container has a shelf life of only three days once it is opened and placed in open container; and though the FSO was informed, he did not bother to take samples from the sealed packets of the 'Corn Meal'. 3. The grievance of the appellants is that the FSO of his own, addressed the sample product as 'Corn Flour' though it was informed to him that sample product was 'corn meal', which is a mixture of various ingredients and he was also informed that it was not meant or available for direct sale to the customers and being used only as intermediary product. At the cost of repetition, the sample product were seized as per Form VA and other formalities were completed and the Food Analyst later on vide report No FSS/378/2014 dated 25.05.2014 held the sample product to be of 'sub standard' quality because the total ash (on dry weight basis) exceeded the prescribed limit of 0.5 %. Accordingly, on receipt of the application from the FSO, the Food Business Operator (FBO) i.e. the appellants were served with the notice as per Rule 3.1.1(6) of the Food Safety and Standards Rules, 2011 alongwith copy of the report of the Food Analyst and giving them an opportunity of being heard. 4. It is the case of the appellants that they appeared before the Adjudicating Officer/ADM through Counsel and filed a representation with supporting documents inter alia also submitting copy of the invoice against which sample product was purchased requesting for impleadment of the supplier but the Adjudicating Officer / ADM rejected the application without a speaking order during the course of proceedings despite the fact that the FSO failed to lead any evidence and the fact that the Food Analyst had not explained as to the process of analysis in contravention of Section 46(3) (I) read with 2.4.2 of the FSS (FPS&FA) Regulation, yet the Ld. Adjudicating Officer/ADM passed the impugned order thereby holding the appellants guilty of Section 26(2) (ii) read with Section 3(1) (zx) of the FSS Act in conjunction with Regulation No. 2.4.7 of (Standards of Corn Flour) of the FSS (FPS&FA) Regulation. Accordingly, consolidated penalty of Rs. 2 Lakhs was imposed upon the respondent Nos. 1 to 3. It is pertinent to mention that respondent No.2 Sh. Ajay Kaul has not cared to file the appeal GROUNDS OF APPEAL: M/S Jubilant Foodworks Ltd vs Sh. Bal Mukund on 13 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19460410/ 2 5. The impugned order has been assailed by the appellants in the present appeal on the grounds that same is perverse, wrong in law besides arbitrary since the Adjudicating Officer/ADM considered the complaint of the FSO as a gospel truth without verification of facts and evidence in support of the complaint; and that the Adjudicating Officer/ADM overruled the fact that sample product was 'corn meal' (a mixture of various ingredients) and not 'corn flour', and therefore, the application of parameters prescribed for the 'corn flour' under Regulation 2.4.7 of FSS (FPS&FA) Regulation, 2011 vitiated the legal sanctity of the report of the Food Analyst as well as report of the referral Laboratory dated 08.09.2014; and that the Adjudicating Officer/ADM failed to appreciate that the sample product was not meant for "direct sale" to the customers and rather the appellants were consumers of the same; and that neither the appellant respondent no. 2 Ajay Kaul nor respondent no. 3 in the original complaint/ appellant no. 2 herein viz., Akash Tyagi were responsible in any manner for the manufacture and storage of the sample product. 6. On the filing of the instant appeal, the operation of the impugned order was stayed subject to the appellants submitting a FDR drawn on any nationalized bank for a initial period of one year and to be renewed till further orders, which has been complied with and notice of the appeal was ordered to be issued to the respondent. Appearance has been put on behalf of the respondents and although no reply as such is filed, the record of the ld Adjudicating Officer is filed and the appeal is opposed.
texts.arguments: Both the directors have opined that there is no reason in holding a sample 0.3%. 15. Much mileage was sought to be taken by the Ld. Counsel for the appellants by referring to defences available vide Section 80 of FSS Act urging that it was not the manufacturer of the sample product but its ends user and that it had no knowledge that the 'Corn Flour' was substandard. M/S Jubilant Foodworks Ltd vs Sh. Bal Mukund on 13 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19460410/ It is but well ordained in legal jurisprudence that no ratio, decision or proposition of law given in a case decided by the superior courts can be read or applied de hor the contextual background or the facts and circumstances of that particular case before the superior court, for which reference can be invited to decision in Padma Sundara Rao v State of Tamil Nadu, (2002) 3 SCC 533. The case law examined from the said perspective, I am afraid the ratio in the case Pepsico India Holdings Private Limited v Food Inspector and Another, 2010 (2) FAC 310 is inapplicable since it was a case where the prosecution was launched under the old Act i.e. Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, where the entire controversy hinged on the fact that no specific limit had been prescribed for Sweetened Carbonated Water under Rule 65 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules 1955. The prosecution was [LEAKAGE_MASK] since no standards were prescribed for packaged drinking water under the relevant regulations/rules and also for the fact that the Central Government had also failed to frame rules to define the laboratories where the sample of M/S Jubilant Foodworks Ltd vs Sh. Bal Mukund on 13 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19460410/ 7 food could be analyzed by the Public Analyst, or to define the validated methods of analysis and the liability of its directors. 19. Reference was invited to decision in Majid Hussain Zamali, Food Inspector v Ramlal Sahu, 1998 (I) FAC 153, wherein a sample of milk was lifted from a tea shop and it was found that the tea vendor was not selling the milk but tea only. Ld. Counsel for the appellants then referred to the decision in B. Govindra Rao vs. V.N. Ashokan, 2003 (2) FAC 123, which was in the context of Section 7 & 16 of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, which provided that sample could only be taken from the article of food which is manufactured, stored or exposed for sale. It was a case where red cherry kept in the store was found to be not intended for sale in a restaurant run by the FBO. 20. Ld. Counsel for the appellants then placed reliance on decision in M.N. Choudhary v State of Bihar, 2007 (I) FAC 106, where a sample of iodized salt was collected from the premises of the Hotel and the prosecution was launched against the General Manager of the Hotel, who was neither the person incharge of the affairs of the store nor of the kitchen of the Hotel, and in the said circumstances, the prosecution against him was [LEAKAGE_MASK] inter alia also on the ground that the storage of iodized salt which was not meant for direct sale was not coming within the mischief of Section 16(1) of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. Likewise, decision in Hindustan Lever Ltd v Nayak, Food Inspector, 2021 (1) FAC 320 was cited, which was a case of selling adulterated flora refined sunflower oil in contravention of Section 7(1) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, and the prosecution launched was [LEAKAGE_MASK] primarily on the ground of not explaining the method of analysis under Section 23(1A) (hh) of PFA Act.
